subject: Social Science
question_text: At the beginning of the nineteenth century, approximately how many steam engines were there in operation across all of England?
option_a: Over 10,000 steam engines
option_b: Around 50,000 steam engines
option_c: Only 5 steam engines
option_d: Only 321 steam engines
correct_answer_text: Only 321 steam engines
explanation: Despite the fame of steam technology, there were no more than 321 steam engines across England in the early nineteenth century (about 80 in cotton, 9 in wool, and the rest in mining and iron works).

subject: Social Science
question_text: According to NCERT, what proportion of India’s total industrial labour force worked in registered factories in 1931?
option_b: Less than 20%
option_c: Nearly 90%
option_d: Around 50%
explanation: NCERT states that only 10 per cent of India’s total industrial labour force worked in registered factories in 1931. The remaining workers were employed in small workshops and household units. This is an India-specific figure and should not be presented as a statistic about England’s technologically advanced sectors.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why did women hand-spinners in Britain violently attack the newly introduced Spinning Jenny machines?
option_a: The machines produced poisonous toxic fumes inside workshops
option_b: The machines were manufactured in France
option_c: Women were legally prohibited from touching metal machinery
option_d: The machine drastically reduced the demand for hand spinning, threatening their traditional source of livelihood and survival
correct_answer_text: The machine drastically reduced the demand for hand spinning, threatening their traditional source of livelihood and survival
explanation: The fear of unemployment and loss of income made hand-spinning women hostile to the Spinning Jenny. Hand-spinners attacked the machines whenever they were introduced into workshops.

subject: Social Science
question_text: By the 1740s, the gross value of trade passing through Surat had fallen from Rs 16 million in the last years of the seventeenth century to no more than:
option_a: Rs 10 million
option_b: Rs 3 million
option_c: Rs 50 million
option_d: Zero
correct_answer_text: Rs 3 million
explanation: NCERT gives the gross value of trade through Surat as Rs 16 million in the last years of the seventeenth century; by the 1740s it had fallen to Rs 3 million. The decline accompanied the weakening of older trading networks as European companies gained concessions and monopoly rights.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why did violent clashes break out between Indian weavers and the Company's Gomasthas in weaving villages?
option_a: Gomasthas were arrogant outsiders who marched into villages with armed sepoys and brutally flogged weavers for delays in delivery
option_b: Gomasthas forced weavers to convert to Christianity
option_c: Gomasthas burned all agricultural fields in the village
option_d: Weavers demanded that Gomasthas marry into their families
correct_answer_text: Gomasthas were arrogant outsiders who marched into villages with armed sepoys and brutally flogged weavers for delays in delivery
explanation: Unlike traditional village merchants who had customary social ties with weavers, Gomasthas were company agents who treated weavers with contempt, using armed sepoys to beat and flog weavers who failed to meet deadlines.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: American Civil War Impact on Indian Weavers
question_text: How did the American Civil War (1861-1865) directly affect handloom weavers in India?
option_a: American cotton exports increased, making Indian raw cotton cheaper and more available
option_b: The American Civil War stopped all textile production in India
option_c: US cotton supplies to Britain were cut off; Britain turned to India, raising Indian raw-cotton exports and prices and making supplies costly for Indian weavers
option_d: The British government prohibited the use of Indian cotton in handlooms
correct_answer_text: US cotton supplies to Britain were cut off; Britain turned to India, raising Indian raw-cotton exports and prices and making supplies costly for Indian weavers
explanation: When the American Civil War disrupted cotton supplies from the United States, Britain turned to India. Indian raw-cotton exports increased and prices rose. Indian weavers then faced shortages and had to buy raw cotton at much higher prices, making weaving less viable.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Early Mills in Ahmedabad and Kanpur
question_text: The Elgin Mill was started in Kanpur in the 1860s, while the first cotton mill of Ahmedabad was set up in:
explanation: NCERT states that the Elgin Mill was started in Kanpur in the 1860s and that the first cotton mill of Ahmedabad was set up a year later, in 1861. The question asks when it was set up, not when production began.

subject: Social Science
question_text: J.N. Tata, the visionary founder of the Tata industrial empire who established the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) in Jamshedpur (1912), accumulated initial capital from:
option_a: Gold mining in South Africa
option_b: Real estate in London
option_c: The China trade and raw cotton exports to Britain
option_d: Exporting tea to Australia
correct_answer_text: The China trade and raw cotton exports to Britain
explanation: Like many early Parsi entrepreneurs in Bombay, J.N. Tata accumulated capital from trade with China and the export of Indian raw cotton to Britain.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Till the First World War, which three large European Managing Agencies controlled a dominant sector of Indian industry including tea plantations, coal mines, and jute mills?
option_a: Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule, and Jardine Skinner & Co.
option_b: East India Company, Hudson Bay Company, and Dutch VOC
option_c: Standard Oil, Ford Motors, and General Electric
option_d: Lloyds Bank, Barclays, and HSBC
correct_answer_text: Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule, and Jardine Skinner & Co.
explanation: Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule, and Jardine Skinner & Co. were three giant British managing agencies that mobilized capital, floated joint-stock companies, and dominated colonial industry in India.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Migrant Origins of Bombay Mill Workers
question_text: In 1911, over 50 percent of the industrial workers in Bombay cotton mills came from the neighbouring agricultural district of:
option_a: Surat
option_b: Pune
option_c: Satara
option_d: Ratnagiri
correct_answer_text: Ratnagiri
explanation: More than 50% of the industrial labour force in the Bombay cotton mills in 1911 was drawn from the nearby coastal agricultural district of Ratnagiri.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Yarn to Cloth Transition in Indian Mills
question_text: Why did early Indian cotton mills focus on spinning yarn rather than weaving cloth, and what forced them to switch to cloth production after 1906?
option_a: Handlooms were prohibited by law until 1906
option_b: Indian mills did not know how to weave cloth until British engineers taught them in 1906
option_c: The British government made cloth production illegal
option_d: They avoided direct competition with Manchester cloth; after 1906, yarn exports to China collapsed as Chinese and Japanese mills expanded, so Indian mills began weaving cloth
correct_answer_text: They avoided direct competition with Manchester cloth; after 1906, yarn exports to China collapsed as Chinese and Japanese mills expanded, so Indian mills began weaving cloth
explanation: Early Indian mills spun coarse yarn to avoid competing with British fabric, exporting yarn to China. When Chinese and Japanese mills took over the China market, Indian mills shifted to weaving finished cloth, aided by the Swadeshi boycott.

subject: Social Science
question_text: After the First World War, why was Manchester never able to recapture its old dominant position in the Indian market?
option_a: The Indian government banned all imports from Great Britain
option_b: Manchester factories were all destroyed by German bombs
option_c: British industry struggled to modernise and compete with the US, Germany and Japan, while Indian industrialists consolidated their position in the home market
option_d: The British navy refused to protect merchant shipping
correct_answer_text: British industry struggled to modernise and compete with the US, Germany and Japan, while Indian industrialists consolidated their position in the home market
explanation: After the First World War, Manchester could not regain its earlier position in the Indian market. NCERT attributes this to Britain’s inability to modernise and compete with the United States, Germany and Japan, alongside the consolidation of local industrialists within the colonies.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How did traditional handloom weavers producing fine varieties of cloth (such as Banarasi and Baluchari sarees) survive competition from machine mills?
option_a: Finer varieties of cloth with complex borders and woven designs could not be easily replicated on mass-production power looms
option_b: They were granted cash subsidies by the British Parliament
option_c: Machine mills agreed never to sell in Indian bazaars
option_d: They sold only to foreign tourists in London
correct_answer_text: Finer varieties of cloth with complex borders and woven designs could not be easily replicated on mass-production power looms
explanation: Machine mills could easily mass-produce coarse cloth, but intricate sarees with woven borders, traditional patterns, and fine muslin could not be imitated by machines. Demand for fine cloth from rich buyers was also stable during famines.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why did manufacturers in late nineteenth-century India use printed calendars as a major advertising medium?
option_a: The British government made calendars the only legal advertising tool
option_b: Unlike newspapers and magazines, calendars were useful to and seen by illiterate consumers in homes, tea shops, and offices all year round
option_c: Calendars were made of silk and could be recycled as clothing
option_d: Newspapers were banned throughout India
correct_answer_text: Unlike newspapers and magazines, calendars were useful to and seen by illiterate consumers in homes, tea shops, and offices all year round
explanation: Calendars were hung on walls in homes, shops, and offices and remained visible day after day to literate and illiterate people alike, ensuring constant brand recall.

subject: Social Science
question_text: What was the message conveyed when foreign and Indian advertisers placed portraits of Indian Nawabs, Emperors, and British royalty on product labels?
option_a: The royalty personally owned the product manufacturing factory
option_b: If royal personages used or approved of the product, its quality was beyond question and consumers should trust it
option_c: Consumers would be arrested if they failed to purchase the product
option_d: The profits were donated directly to royal charities
correct_answer_text: If royal personages used or approved of the product, its quality was beyond question and consumers should trust it
explanation: Royal figures conveyed prestige, royal patronage, and supreme quality: if the Emperor or Prince was shown using the commodity, its excellence was guaranteed.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In 1911, what percentage of India’s total industrial labour force worked in registered factories?
option_b: Over 65%
option_c: Nearly 85%
option_d: Around 40%
explanation: NCERT states that 5 per cent of India’s total industrial labour force worked in registered factories in 1911, rising to 10 per cent by 1931. Most industrial workers therefore continued to work in small workshops and household units.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In textile production, what does the process of 'carding' involve?
option_a: Weaving threads together to make finished cloth
option_b: Dyeing yarn in bright chemical colours
option_c: Stamping prices and company trademarks on cloth bundles
option_d: The process in which raw cotton or wool fibres are prepared and untangled prior to spinning
correct_answer_text: The process in which raw cotton or wool fibres are prepared and untangled prior to spinning
explanation: Carding is the essential preliminary process where tangled raw fibres (cotton or wool) are cleaned, straightened, and prepared for spinning into yarn.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How did the role of the Jobber change over time as he gained power over job-seeking villagers?
option_a: He surrendered his job to form the Indian National Congress
option_b: He became the managing director of the British managing agency
option_c: He began demanding money, gifts, and kickbacks for securing jobs and started controlling the personal lives of workers
option_d: He was replaced entirely by computer algorithm testing
correct_answer_text: He began demanding money, gifts, and kickbacks for securing jobs and started controlling the personal lives of workers
explanation: As the demand for factory jobs outstripped vacancies, the Jobber acquired enormous informal authority, demanding bribes, gifts, and personal subservience in exchange for mill employment.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): Even before factories began to appear in England and Europe, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market.\nReason (R): This phase of industrial history is referred to by historians as proto-industrialisation, and it was based entirely in rural cottage households rather than factories.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Proto-industrialisation demonstrated that industrial manufacturing for global markets existed long before mechanized urban factories emerged, organized across rural cottage networks. Both are true and (R) explains (A).

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): Merchants could not easily expand textile production inside seventeenth-century European towns.\nReason (R): Urban craft and trade guilds were powerful associations that trained craftspeople, controlled production, regulated competition and prices, and restricted entry into particular trades.

NCERT describes guilds as associations that trained craftspeople, maintained control over production, regulated competition and prices, and restricted entry into trades, making it difficult for merchants to expand production within towns.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): In Victorian Britain, industrialists had no widespread eagerness to replace human workers with machines.\nReason (R): Poor peasants and vagrants moved to cities in large numbers searching for jobs, resulting in an abundance of cheap human labour.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: When labour was plentiful and wages were low, industrialists had little economic reason to invest in expensive machinery that carried high capital depreciation and repair costs. Both are true and (R) explains (A).

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): In nineteenth-century America, industrialists were far keener on using mechanical power than their British counterparts.\nReason (R): Unlike Britain where labour was abundant, the United States faced an acute shortage of human labour.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Labour scarcity in America drove rapid mechanization because industrialists could not hire cheap manual workers, whereas British manufacturers relied on plentiful cheap labour. Both are true and (R) explains (A).

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): By the mid-eighteenth century, the older ports of Surat and Hooghly declined while Bombay and Calcutta grew.\nReason (R): European companies gradually gained concessions and monopoly rights to trade, weakening the older merchant networks; Bombay and Calcutta later grew as trading ports in the colonial economy.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): Unlike earlier supply merchants, Gomasthas had no social link with weaving villages.\nReason (R): Gomasthas were paid outsiders who acted arrogantly and used armed sepoys and peons to punish weavers for delays in delivery.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion. Earlier supply merchants often lived in weaving villages and had long-term social relationships with weavers. Gomasthas were paid Company employees and outsiders without those established village ties. Their arrogant conduct and use of sepoys and peons describe how they enforced Company demands; those actions do not logically explain the absence of prior social ties.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): In the nineteenth century, Indian textiles faced severe decline in both foreign and domestic markets.\nReason (R): Britain imposed high import duties on Indian cloth entering Britain, while British machine-made cotton goods entered India tariff-free.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Tariff asymmetry crushed Indian weaving: Indian exports to Britain were blocked by heavy protective duties, while cheap Manchester factory cloth flooded Indian bazaars without import duties. Both are true and (R) explains (A).

subject: Social Science
question_text: Assertion (A): During the First World War, Manchester imports into India declined dramatically.\nReason (R): British factories were fully mobilized to produce war supplies (army uniforms, tents, artillery, and boots) to meet the military needs of the Allied powers.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: British wartime mobilization diverted Manchester's capacity away from commercial export to imperial military supplies, creating a huge domestic supply void in India filled by Indian textile mills. Both are true and (R) explains (A).

option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

NCERT says that demand for finer varieties bought by the well-to-do was more stable and that the rich could buy these products even when the poor starved. This should not be generalised to mean that every wealthy buyer’s purchasing power was completely unaffected by famine.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 1: Proto-Industrialization & Rural Family Labour
question_text: Case Study 1 (Q11-Q13): In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, merchants moved into rural Europe, establishing commercial networks with peasant families.\n\nQ11: How did proto-industrial production help peasant families maintain their livelihoods?
option_a: It allowed peasants to purchase all land in the country
option_b: It made farming completely unnecessary
option_c: It granted peasants royal patents over inventions
option_d: It allowed peasants to cultivate their small plots of land while utilizing surplus family labour to earn supplementary cash wages
correct_answer_text: It allowed peasants to cultivate their small plots of land while utilizing surplus family labour to earn supplementary cash wages
explanation: Proto-industrial production allowed peasant households to stay in their villages, farm their smallholdings, and employ all family members (women, elders, children) in spinning and weaving.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 1: Proto-Industrialization & Rural Family Labour
question_text: Case Study 1 (Continued): The stages of cloth production were dispersed across multiple locations.\n\nQ12: In what sequence did wool travel during proto-industrial production before reaching London?
option_a: From London -> weaver -> spinner -> sheep farm
option_b: From dyer -> wool stapler -> weaver -> spinner
option_c: From wool stapler -> spinner -> weaver -> fuller -> dyer in London
option_d: From fuller -> dyer -> spinner -> stapler
correct_answer_text: From wool stapler -> spinner -> weaver -> fuller -> dyer in London
explanation: The proto-industrial sequence described by NCERT was wool stapler, spinner, weaver, fuller and then dyer. The fuller gathered the cloth by pleating; finishing was done in London before the export merchant sold the cloth in the international market.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 1: Proto-Industrialization & Rural Family Labour
question_text: Case Study 1 (Continued): How was proto-industrial production controlled and financed?
option_a: It was run as state-owned enterprises by the British Crown
option_b: It was controlled and financed by merchants, while the goods were produced by vast numbers of producers working within family households
option_c: It was managed by village church councils
option_d: It was financed exclusively by French banks
correct_answer_text: It was controlled and financed by merchants, while the goods were produced by vast numbers of producers working within family households
explanation: The entire proto-industrial network was commercialized and financed by private merchants who coordinated thousands of cottage producers working from their homes.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 2: The Plight of Weavers Under the Company
question_text: Case Study 2 (Q14-Q16): Before the 1760s, the East India Company had struggled to secure regular supplies of cotton textiles from Indian weavers.\n\nQ14: Why had the Company previously faced stiff competition in procuring Indian cloth?
option_a: Weaving was strictly forbidden by the Mughal Emperor
option_b: Indian cotton was too coarse for European markets
option_c: British merchants refused to buy cloth from Hindu weavers
option_d: French, Dutch, and Portuguese traders, along with local Indian merchants, actively bid against each other in the open market
correct_answer_text: French, Dutch, and Portuguese traders, along with local Indian merchants, actively bid against each other in the open market
explanation: Multiple European companies (French, Dutch, Portuguese) and Indian merchants competed fiercely, allowing weavers to negotiate the best price for their woven cloth.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 2: The Plight of Weavers Under the Company
question_text: Case Study 2 (Continued): After the Company eliminated competitors and established monopoly control through the system of advances:\n\nQ15: Why were weavers unable to cultivate their agricultural land once they took Company advances?
option_a: The Company confiscated all their farming tools
option_b: All agricultural land was flooded by irrigation canals
option_c: Weaving required the intensive labour of the entire family (men, women, and children), leaving no time to tend agricultural fields
option_d: Landlords evicted any weaver who accepted a Company advance
correct_answer_text: Weaving required the intensive labour of the entire family (men, women, and children), leaving no time to tend agricultural fields
explanation: Because the loans tied weavers to produce heavy quotas of cloth, weaving consumed every waking hour of the weaver and his entire family, forcing them to lease out or abandon their farm plots.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 2: The Plight of Weavers Under the Company
question_text: Case Study 2 (Continued): How did desperate Indian weavers resist the oppression of the Company's Gomasthas?
option_a: They deserted their villages, migrated to other districts where they had relatives, or revolted alongside village traders against the Company
option_b: They destroyed all British warships in Calcutta
option_c: They set up mechanized cotton mills in Paris
option_d: They petitioned the Russian Tsar for military intervention
correct_answer_text: They deserted their villages, migrated to other districts where they had relatives, or revolted alongside village traders against the Company
explanation: In many villages across Carnatic and Bengal, weavers deserted their native villages en masse, setting up looms in districts where they had family ties, or occasionally clashed violently with gomasthas.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 3: The Jobber and Mill Recruitment
question_text: Case Study 3 (Q17-Q18): Even as factories expanded across Bombay, Kanpur, and Calcutta, securing a factory job was difficult for rural migrants.\n\nQ17: Why was it difficult for poor jobseekers to get mill employment directly?
option_a: Jobseekers were required to have university degrees in engineering
option_b: Factory owners refused to hire anyone from rural areas
option_c: British law made employment illegal without a passport
option_d: The number of jobseekers was always far greater than the available vacancies, and mills had strict entry restrictions
correct_answer_text: The number of jobseekers was always far greater than the available vacancies, and mills had strict entry restrictions
explanation: Surplus agricultural labour resulted in thousands of rural migrants crowding mill gates, far outstripping the number of available jobs.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 3: The Jobber and Mill Recruitment
question_text: Case Study 3 (Continued): Industrialists hired a trusted veteran worker called the Jobber.\n\nQ18: What assistance did the Jobber typically provide to new migrants from his village?

option_b: He built free bungalows for them in posh areas
option_c: He sent their children to English schools in London
option_d: He provided them with steam cars for daily commuting
correct_answer_text: He promised them jobs, helped them settle in the strange city, and provided temporary loans during times of financial crisis
explanation: The Jobber acted as an essential patron for village migrants, helping them navigate the harsh urban landscape, providing emergency loans, and vouching for them at the factory gate.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 4: Market Creation & Advertising Strategies
question_text: Case Study 4 (Q19-Q20): When British manufacturers took over the Indian market, they had to create new wants and persuade people to buy machine goods.\n\nQ19: What was the primary purpose of the bold text 'Made in Manchester' printed on cloth labels?
option_a: To warn buyers that the cloth was inflammable
option_b: To serve as a mark of superior quality and inspire confidence in Indian buyers
option_c: To show that the cloth had been taxed by the Mughal court
option_d: To indicate that the cloth was meant exclusively for export to China
correct_answer_text: To serve as a mark of superior quality and inspire confidence in Indian buyers
explanation: 'Made in Manchester' was presented as a badge of quality and prestige, assuring Indian buyers that they were purchasing genuine, top-quality British machine-made cloth.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Study 4: Market Creation & Advertising Strategies
question_text: Case Study 4 (Continued): Advertisements served a dual purpose in nineteenth and twentieth-century India.\n\nQ20: How did advertisements transform into vehicles of the nationalist message of Swadeshi during the Indian freedom struggle?
option_a: Advertisements were used to transmit secret military coded messages to guerrillas
option_b: Advertisements urged consumers to stop wearing clothes completely
option_c: Indian manufacturers explicitly advertised buying domestic goods as a patriotic contribution to the nation's economic independence
option_d: Advertisements called for an immediate boycott of all Indian railways
correct_answer_text: Indian manufacturers explicitly advertised buying domestic goods as a patriotic contribution to the nation's economic independence
explanation: Indian manufacturers used commercial advertisements to champion the nationalist cause: purchasing Indian-made goods was positioned as a patriotic duty to support the nation's struggle for Swaraj.

subject: Social Science
question_text: What is the oldest printed book of Japan, printed in AD 868 containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations?
option_a: Buddhist Diamond Sutra
option_b: Tale of Genji
option_c: Bible
option_d: Ukiyo-e Chronicles
correct_answer_text: Buddhist Diamond Sutra
explanation: The Buddhist Diamond Sutra, printed in Japan in AD 868, is universally recognized as the oldest surviving dated printed book in the world. Discovered inside the Dunhuang caves, this remarkable artifact consists of six woodblock-printed sheets of mulberry paper containing Buddhist sutra Sanskrit-Chinese calligraphy text alongside an intricate woodcut frontispiece illustration depicting the Buddha preaching to his elderly disciple Subhuti. It reflects the ancient East Asian mastery of block printing centuries before Europe.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In 1295, which great Italian explorer returned to Italy after years of exploration in China and brought back the knowledge of woodblock printing?
option_a: Christopher Columbus
option_b: Vasco da Gama
option_c: Marco Polo
option_d: Amerigo Vespucci
correct_answer_text: Marco Polo
explanation: In 1295, the Venetian merchant explorer Marco Polo returned to Venice after spending over seventeen years exploring China, the Silk Route, and the imperial Mongol court of Kublai Khan. Among the sophisticated Eastern technologies he introduced to Italy was the Chinese art of woodblock printing. Italian craftsmen and book publishers embraced this technique, mass-producing printed playing cards, religious prints, and inexpensive paper books, which rapidly diffused across trade routes into Germany, France, and the Netherlands.

subject: Social Science
question_text: What was the first major book printed by Johann Gutenberg on his movable metal-type printing press in Mainz, completed around 1455?
option_a: The Diamond Sutra
option_b: Ninety-Five Theses
option_c: The Canterbury Tales
option_d: The Bible
correct_answer_text: The Bible
explanation: Johann Gutenberg developed a mechanised movable-metal-type printing press in Mainz in the mid-fifteenth century. The famous 42-line Latin Bible, now known as the Gutenberg Bible, was completed around 1455. The press was developed before the Bible was completed; the year 1448 should not be presented as the date of the first Bible's printing.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In 1517, the religious reformer Martin Luther wrote 'Ninety-Five Theses' criticizing many of the practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church, posting it on the church door at:
option_a: Mainz
option_b: Wittenberg
option_c: Frankfurt
option_d: Rome
correct_answer_text: Wittenberg
explanation: In 1517, the German Augustinian monk and theology professor Martin Luther wrote his fiery 'Ninety-Five Theses' (Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences) condemning corrupt Roman Catholic Church practices, particularly the commercial sale of papal indulgences for remission of sins. Luther posted a printed copy on the heavy oak doors of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg, challenging scholars to a public theological debate. Printed vernacular copies were rapidly reproduced and circulated across Germany, igniting the Reformation.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Who declared that 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one'?
option_a: Johann Gutenberg
option_b: Martin Luther
option_c: Erasmus
option_d: Louis-Sébastien Mercier
correct_answer_text: Martin Luther
explanation: Deeply awed by the revolutionary speed with which his German translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies in a fortnight, Protestant reformer Martin Luther famously declared: 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.' Luther recognized that Gutenberg's mechanized movable press was an unstoppable democratic equalizer that broke the Catholic Church's Latin monopoly on biblical scriptures, enabling ordinary literate citizens to read, interpret, and practice religious faith independently without papal priests.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Who was Menocchio, hauled before the Roman Catholic Inquisition in the sixteenth century and executed for heresy?
option_a: A German monk who translated the New Testament
option_b: A French royal censor who banned Voltaire's writings
option_c: A Dutch cartographer who drew maps of the Americas
option_d: An Italian miller who reinterpreted the Bible and developed radical views on God and Creation
correct_answer_text: An Italian miller who reinterpreted the Bible and developed radical views on God and Creation
explanation: Menocchio (Domenico Scandella) was a literate village miller from northern Italy who devoured vernacular books, folk tales, and popular translations of the Bible made available by the 16th-century print revolution. Comparing printed texts with his daily rustic experiences, Menocchio formulated a radical, heretical cosmology: he declared that God and the universe emerged from primordial chaos just as maggots and cheese emerge from curdled milk. Alarmed by his subversive views, the Roman Catholic Inquisition arrested, tortured, and executed him.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Alarmed by heretical literature and independent interpretations of faith, the Roman Catholic Church began maintaining the official 'Index of Prohibited Books' from:
explanation: The explosion of vernacular printed literature, Protestant theology, and popular anti-clerical tracts deeply alarmed the Roman Catholic Church hierarchy. Fearing that uncontrolled print gave uneducated commoners and heretics the dangerous power to question religious dogma, church authorities instituted strict pre-publication censorship controls over European printers and booksellers. In 1558 (under Pope Paul IV), the Roman Catholic Church officially published the first authoritative 'Index of Prohibited Books' (Index Librorum Prohibitorum).

subject: Social Science
question_text: In England, small, cheap pocket-sized booklets sold by travelling pedlars for a single penny were known as:
option_a: Bibliothèque Bleue
option_b: Almanacs
option_c: Chapbooks
option_d: Belles-lettres
correct_answer_text: Chapbooks
explanation: In eighteenth-century England, the dramatic rise in working-class literacy fueled an insatiable popular appetite for cheap, accessible reading materials. Publishers responded by producing 'chapbooks'—pocket-sized booklets printed on coarse paper and priced at just one penny (a penny chapbook) so that even impoverished urban artisans and farmhands could afford them. These booklets were carried across remote countryside villages by itinerant pedlars known as 'chapmen', featuring folklore, murder ballads, historical tales, and almanacs.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In France, cheap, low-priced popular books bound in low-cost blue paper covers were called:
option_a: Chapbooks
option_b: Novels
option_c: Pamphlets
option_d: Bibliothèque Bleue
correct_answer_text: Bibliothèque Bleue
explanation: In eighteenth-century France, publishers established a wildly successful mass-market publishing genre known as the 'Bibliothèque Bleue' (the Blue Library). These were compact, low-priced pocketbooks printed on inexpensive, coarse grayish paper and bound in flimsy, distinctive blue sugar-paper covers. Distributed across rural provinces by travelling colporteurs (pedlars), they catered to newly literate peasants and urban wage-earners, containing abridged chivalric romances, moral allegories, folk tales, and practical advice.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Mercier on the Power of Print
question_text: Which French eighteenth-century novelist proclaimed: ‘Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world! Tremble before the virtuous writer!’?
option_a: Louis-Sébastien Mercier
option_b: Voltaire
option_c: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
option_d: Denis Diderot
correct_answer_text: Louis-Sébastien Mercier
explanation: Louis-Sébastien Mercier expressed confidence in the power of print and the written word to challenge despotism. The phrase in the NCERT text is ‘virtuous writer’, not ‘virtual writer’.

subject: Social Science
question_text: By the mid-nineteenth century, who perfected the power-driven cylindrical press capable of printing 8,000 sheets per hour, specially used for newspapers?
option_a: Johann Gutenberg of Mainz
option_b: Richard M. Hoe of New York
option_c: James Watt of Birmingham
option_d: Isaac Pitman of London
correct_answer_text: Richard M. Hoe of New York
explanation: By the mid-nineteenth century, the insatiable global demand for daily newspapers and commercial periodicals demanded mechanical breakthroughs. Richard March Hoe of New York perfected the rotary cylindrical printing press in the 1840s. By mounting movable curved type onto a massive revolving central cylinder that pressed against smaller impression rollers, Hoe's power-driven rotary press printed up to 8,000 newspaper sheets per hour, shattering old flat-bed limits and ushering in modern mass-circulation daily journalism.

subject: Social Science
question_text: The printing press first came to India in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century with:
option_a: British East India Company merchants
option_b: French traders in Pondicherry
option_c: Portuguese Jesuit missionaries
option_d: Dutch navigators in Cochin
correct_answer_text: Portuguese Jesuit missionaries
explanation: The printing press made its historical debut in the Indian subcontinent in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century, brought by Portuguese Jesuit missionaries. Jesuit priests mastered indigenous Indian languages to preach Christian doctrine to coastal populations: they printed the first Konkani and Marathi religious catechisms and grammars by 1556–1579. By 1674, approximately fifty theological books had been printed in Konkani and Kanara, marking the formal arrival of European typography on Indian soil.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In 1780, who began editing the ‘Bengal Gazette’, a private weekly English newspaper described as ‘a commercial paper open to all, but influenced by none’?
option_a: Warren Hastings
option_b: William Bolts
option_c: James Augustus Hickey
option_d: Gangadhar Bhattacharya
correct_answer_text: James Augustus Hickey
explanation: From 1780, James Augustus Hickey edited the Bengal Gazette, a weekly newspaper. It represented private English-language printing enterprise in India and carried advertisements as well as gossip about Company officials.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which influential weekly newspaper did Raja Rammohun Roy publish from 1821 to debate social and religious reforms?
option_a: Samachar Chandrika
option_b: Sambad Kaumudi
option_c: Kesari
option_d: Rast Goftar
correct_answer_text: Sambad Kaumudi
explanation: Raja Rammohun Roy, the pioneering reformist often hailed as the father of modern Indian renaissance, founded the historic weekly Bengali newspaper 'Sambad Kaumudi' in 1821. Roy utilized print as a powerful weapon of rational social reform, publishing scholarly arguments dismantling cruel orthodox Hindu customs—particularly the brutal practice of Sati (widow-burning), female infanticide, child marriage, and hereditary caste untouchability. In response, Hindu conservatives launched the rival weekly 'Samachar Chandrika' in 1822.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Founded in 1867, which Islamic seminary in North India published thousands of fatwas guiding Muslim conduct in daily life and explaining Islamic doctrines?
option_a: Aligarh Muslim University
option_b: Nadwatul Ulama Lucknow
option_c: Jamia Millia Islamia
option_d: Deoband Seminary
correct_answer_text: Deoband Seminary
explanation: Founded in 1867 in the Saharanpur district of Uttar Pradesh amidst post-1857 colonial anxieties, the Deoband Seminary (Darul Uloom Deoband) mobilized modern print technology to preserve orthodox Islamic theological traditions. The seminary utilized high-speed lithographic printing presses to mass-produce and distribute thousands upon thousands of authoritative legal rulings ('fatwas') in Urdu, instructing Muslim households on ethical personal conduct, daily prayers, halal living, and biblical interpretations under non-Muslim colonial rule.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Who wrote 'Amar Jiban' (1876), the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language, having learned to read secretly in her kitchen?
option_a: Rashsundari Debi
option_b: Kailashbashini Debi
option_c: Tarabai Shinde
option_d: Pandita Ramabai
correct_answer_text: Rashsundari Debi
explanation: Rashsundari Debi, an orthodox Vaishnava housewife in rural East Bengal (now Bangladesh), shattered rigorous patriarchal taboos by secretly teaching herself to read and write in her smoky kitchen by the flickering light of cooking fires, stealing glimpses of manuscripts while cooking. In 1876, she published 'Amar Jiban' ('My Life'), which holds the historic distinction of being the first full-length autobiography ever published in the Bengali language, offering a moving account of women's domestic subjugation.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In 1882 in Maharashtra, who published 'Stripurushtulna' ('A Comparison Between Women and Men') criticizing the social inequalities and double standards imposed on women?
option_a: Pandita Ramabai
option_b: Savitribai Phule
option_c: Tarabai Shinde
option_d: Anandibai Joshi
correct_answer_text: Tarabai Shinde
explanation: In 1882 in Maharashtra, the fearless feminist and social reformer Tarabai Shinde published a blistering, radical Marathi polemical treatise titled 'Stripurushtulna' ('A Comparison Between Women and Men'). Sparked by upper-caste condemnation of an ostracized young widow who had terminated an unwanted pregnancy, Shinde used piercing vernacular prose to deconstruct patriarchal double standards, attacking male privileges, religious orthodoxies, and societal misogyny that blamed women for crimes committed by men.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In 1873, Jyotirao Phule published ‘Gulamgiri’ (‘Slavery’), exposing caste oppression and dedicating his book to:
option_a: The Americans who fought to abolish black slavery in the American Civil War
option_b: The French revolutionaries of 1789
option_c: The factory workers of Manchester
option_d: The peasants of the Russian revolution
correct_answer_text: The Americans who fought to abolish black slavery in the American Civil War
explanation: Jyotirao Phule published Gulamgiri in 1873 and dedicated it to the people of the United States who had fought to abolish slavery. The Library of Congress catalogue records the publication year as 1873. Some NCERT-derived material has circulated the year 1871; the primary bibliographic record supports 1873, so this question uses the documented publication year.

subject: Social Science
question_text: The repressive Vernacular Press Act passed by the British colonial government in 1878 was modeled on the:
option_a: Prussian Censorship Decree
option_b: Irish Press Laws
option_c: Napoleonic Code
option_d: American Sedition Act
correct_answer_text: Irish Press Laws
explanation: In 1878, the colonial government under Viceroy Lord Lytton passed the repressive Vernacular Press Act to muzzle the burgeoning nationalist movement. Modelled directly on the authoritarian Irish Press Laws, the Act empowered British district magistrates to censor vernacular newspapers, demand financial security deposits, and confiscate printing presses, paper, and equipment if any journal published content deemed seditious or critical of British colonial governance, exempting English-language colonial papers.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which nationalist leader was imprisoned in 1908 for writing with deep sympathy in his Marathi newspaper 'Kesari' about deported Punjab revolutionaries, sparking nationwide strikes?
option_a: Lala Lajpat Rai
option_b: Bipin Chandra Pal
option_c: Gopal Krishna Gokhale
option_d: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
correct_answer_text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
explanation: Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, the staunch radical leader of the Indian National Congress, mobilized the vernacular press to ignite militant anti-colonial resistance. Editing the influential Marathi weekly newspaper 'Kesari', Tilak penned scathing, fearless editorials in 1908 sympathizing with Bengal revolutionaries and condemning British atrocities in the wake of the Muzaffarpur bombing. Tilak was arrested for sedition, convicted by a biased colonial court, and sentenced to six years of hard labor in Mandalay prison in Burma.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In imperial China, traditional woodblock printed books were folded and stitched at the side as an 'accordion book' because:
option_a: Chinese calligraphy characters could only be read horizontally
option_b: The porous and thin paper could not be printed on both sides
option_c: Emperors ordered that all books must look like musical instruments
option_d: Glue was legally prohibited in Chinese publishing
correct_answer_text: The porous and thin paper could not be printed on both sides
explanation: Because traditional Chinese paper was thin and porous, ink seeped through, making two-sided printing impossible; therefore sheets were folded and bound as accordion books.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which Japanese artist was a prominent master of ‘ukiyo-e’ (‘pictures of the floating world’), depicting ordinary urban life in Edo (Tokyo)?
option_a: Kitagawa Utamaro
option_b: Hokusai
option_c: Hiroshige
option_d: Kawabata
correct_answer_text: Kitagawa Utamaro
explanation: Kitagawa Utamaro was a prominent Japanese artist associated with ukiyo-e woodblock prints. Ukiyo-e was a broader artistic tradition rather than an art form invented by Utamaro alone.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why did some wealthy European aristocrats in the fifteenth century initially regard printed books as inferior to handwritten manuscripts?
option_a: Printed books were printed only in Latin, which aristocrats did not understand
option_b: The Church threatened to excommunicate anyone owning a printed book
option_c: Gutenberg refused to sell books to aristocrats
option_d: They associated printed books with cheaper mass production and preferred prestigious handwritten manuscripts, often produced on expensive vellum
correct_answer_text: They associated printed books with cheaper mass production and preferred prestigious handwritten manuscripts, often produced on expensive vellum
explanation: Some wealthy readers initially valued handwritten manuscripts as prestigious objects and regarded early printed books as comparatively cheap or mechanically produced. The distinction was one of status and perceived quality, not a universal refusal by all aristocrats to own printed books.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How did Johann Gutenberg's upbringing and craft skills enable him to invent movable metal type?
option_a: He studied engineering at the Sorbonne university
option_b: He discovered movable wooden type in an Egyptian pyramid
option_c: He was a master goldsmith experienced with making lead trinket moulds, and adapted the screw design of the agricultural olive and wine press
option_d: He worked in a paper manufacturing factory in Venice
correct_answer_text: He was a master goldsmith experienced with making lead trinket moulds, and adapted the screw design of the agricultural olive and wine press
explanation: Gutenberg combined his experience in olive/wine presses (providing the press mechanism) with his goldsmithing expertise in lead/tin casting to invent durable movable metal type characters.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How did early printers bridge the cultural gap between the small literate minority and the vast illiterate majority in early modern Europe?
option_a: By offering free university evening classes to all peasants
option_b: By printing popular ballads, folk tales, and religious texts illustrated with pictures that were recited and sung aloud in village taverns and gatherings
option_c: By producing books with audio recordings
option_d: By printing books only in sign language
correct_answer_text: By printing popular ballads, folk tales, and religious texts illustrated with pictures that were recited and sung aloud in village taverns and gatherings
explanation: Because most common people could not read, publishers printed illustrated ballads and folktales that could be sung or recited aloud in communal taverns, seamlessly blending oral culture with print.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why did the Latin scholar and Catholic reformer Erasmus express deep anxiety about the flood of printed books in his 1508 work 'Adages'?
option_a: He wanted all printing presses to be converted into paper recycling mills
option_b: He believed books made human beings physically blind
option_c: He feared that uncontrolled printing filled the world with ignorant, scandalous, irreligious, and seditious books that degraded scholarly value
option_d: He feared that Latin would be replaced by Chinese
correct_answer_text: He feared that uncontrolled printing filled the world with ignorant, scandalous, irreligious, and seditious books that degraded scholarly value
explanation: Erasmus worried that the unrestrained proliferation of printing flooded the world with swarms of worthless, defamatory, and heretical books that drowned out true scholarly and religious wisdom.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How did print popularize the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire, Rousseau, and Thomas Paine in the eighteenth century?
option_a: Their books were mass printed in affordable editions, promoting critical reason and challenging superstition and monarchical despotism
option_b: Their ideas were carved on stone monuments across Paris
option_c: Their books were read only by the King and Queen of France
option_d: Their writings were taught exclusively in military academies
correct_answer_text: Their books were mass printed in affordable editions, promoting critical reason and challenging superstition and monarchical despotism
explanation: Enlightenment thinkers' writings were printed widely in pocketbooks and pamphlets, enabling ordinary readers to judge royal authority, church dogma, and tradition through the prism of reason.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In pre-revolutionary France of the 1780s, what was the common theme of popular satirical cartoons and caricatures circulating in Paris?
option_a: French peasants conquering Great Britain
option_b: British soldiers running away from French fleets
option_c: Scientists discovering steam locomotives
option_d: Monarchy and nobility indulging in lavish pleasures while common people starved in misery
correct_answer_text: Monarchy and nobility indulging in lavish pleasures while common people starved in misery
explanation: Underground print literature circulated cartoons and caricatures showing the royalty immersed in selfish hedonistic pleasures while common folk bore crushing tax burdens, eroding royal legitimacy.

subject: Social Science
question_text: What important institutional milestone for children's literature occurred in France in 1857?
option_a: All children under ten were banned from touching books
option_b: School textbooks were replaced by illustrated newspapers
option_c: Comic books were declared compulsory in all primary schools
option_d: A press devoted exclusively to literature for children was established
correct_answer_text: A press devoted exclusively to literature for children was established
explanation: In 1857, a dedicated children's printing press was founded in France to publish both new stories and classic fairy tales adapted for young readers.

subject: Social Science
question_text: When the Grimm Brothers in Germany collected traditional folk tales from peasants, what editorial changes did they make before publishing them in 1812?
option_a: They translated all stories into Latin verse
option_b: They converted every human character into an animal
option_c: They edited out vulgarities and content considered unsuitable for children and elite bourgeois sensibilities
option_d: They set all fairy tales in ancient Rome
correct_answer_text: They edited out vulgarities and content considered unsuitable for children and elite bourgeois sensibilities
explanation: The Grimm Brothers spent years gathering folk stories directly from peasants, but carefully filtered and sanitized the tales to remove sexual references, coarse peasant humour, and material deemed inappropriate for children.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which prominent nineteenth-century women novelists redefined the concept of womanhood through characters with intellect, independent will, and moral determination?
option_a: Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters, and George Eliot
option_b: Virginia Woolf, Agatha Christie, and Sylvia Plath
option_c: Mary Shelley, Louisa May Alcott, and Emily Dickinson
option_d: Queen Victoria, Florence Nightingale, and Joan of Arc
correct_answer_text: Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters, and George Eliot
explanation: Novels by Jane Austen, Charlotte and Emily Brontë, and George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans) portrayed women not merely as passive decorative domestic figures, but as strong, reflective, and morally resolute individuals.

subject: Social Science
question_text: During the economic hardship of the 1930s, what publishing approach helped keep books affordable for readers?
option_a: By distributing books free of cost through government food rations
option_b: By introducing inexpensive book series and cheaper editions
option_c: By printing books only on discarded cloth rags
option_d: By stopping book publishing completely
correct_answer_text: By introducing inexpensive book series and cheaper editions
explanation: During the 1930s, publishers introduced cheap series of books to attract readers whose purchasing power had been reduced by economic hardship. The NCERT account refers to cheap book series; it does not require the narrower claim that this was specifically a paperback innovation.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Catholic Missionary Printing in South India
question_text: In South India, Catholic missionaries printed the first Tamil book at Cochin in 1579, and the first Malayalam book in:
explanation: Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin, and in 1713 the first Malayalam book was printed by them.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Who brought out the weekly 'Bengal Gazette' in English, becoming the first Indian to publish a newspaper in India?
option_a: Gangadhar Bhattacharya
option_b: Raja Rammohun Roy
option_c: Dwarkanath Tagore
option_d: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
correct_answer_text: Gangadhar Bhattacharya
explanation: Gangadhar Bhattacharya, a close associate of Raja Rammohun Roy, published the weekly 'Bengal Gazette', making him the first Indian to bring out a newspaper.

subject: Social Science
question_text: To counter Raja Rammohun Roy's reformist arguments in 'Sambad Kaumudi', the Hindu orthodox establishment founded which newspaper in 1821?
option_a: Bombay Samachar
option_b: Jam-i-Jahan Numa
option_c: Amrita Bazar Patrika
option_d: Samachar Chandrika
correct_answer_text: Samachar Chandrika
explanation: The Hindu orthodox lobby commissioned 'Samachar Chandrika' to defend traditional customs like sati and oppose the rationalist social reforms advocated by Rammohun Roy.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Vernacular Presses Naval Kishore & Shri Venkateshwar
question_text: Which two famous publishing houses founded in the late nineteenth century published countless vernacular religious texts like Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas across India?
option_a: Oxford University Press and Cambridge University Press
option_b: Baptist Mission Press and Asiatic Society Press
option_c: Naval Kishore Press in Lucknow and Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay
option_d: Penguin Books and Macmillan Press
correct_answer_text: Naval Kishore Press in Lucknow and Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay
explanation: Naval Kishore Press (Lucknow) and Shri Venkateshwar Press (Bombay) were legendary vernacular printing powerhouses that mass-printed religious scriptures in Hindi, Urdu, and other regional tongues.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In nineteenth-century Calcutta, which central district became famous as the thriving hub for printing cheap popular books, woodcuts, and illustrated almanacs?
option_a: Chowringhee
option_b: Alipore
option_c: Battala
option_d: Howrah
correct_answer_text: Battala
explanation: The Battala area in north Calcutta was the bustling center of popular Bengali print culture, producing cheap mythological tracts, scandalous tales, and woodcut engravings sold by pedlars.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Kashibaba Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal
question_text: In 1938, a Kanpur mill worker named Kashibaba wrote and published a famous booklet exposing the links between caste and class exploitation titled:
option_a: Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal
option_b: Gulamgiri
option_c: Stripurushtulna
option_d: Sacchi Kavitayan
correct_answer_text: Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal
explanation: Kashibaba, a Kanpur mill worker, authored 'Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal' in 1938 to expose the deep nexus between caste oppression and capitalist class exploitation.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In 1835, urgent representations by editors of English and vernacular newspapers led Governor-General William Bentinck and which law member to restore freedom of the Indian press?
option_a: Lord Lytton
option_b: Lord Curzon
option_c: Lord Wellesley
option_d: Thomas Macaulay
correct_answer_text: Thomas Macaulay
explanation: Thomas Macaulay formulated liberal press rules in 1835, revising earlier restrictive regulations and restoring substantive freedom to Indian and Anglo-Indian newspapers.

subject: Social Science
question_text: To escape the draconian censorship provisions of the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 overnight, which prominent nationalist newspaper switched its language from Bengali to English?
option_a: The Hindu
option_b: Amrita Bazar Patrika
option_c: The Statesman
option_d: Kesari
correct_answer_text: Amrita Bazar Patrika
explanation: Because the Vernacular Press Act applied exclusively to non-English (vernacular) newspapers, Amrita Bazar Patrika cleverly morphed from a Bengali newspaper into an English newspaper overnight to escape government censorship.
