option_d: Transferring state revenues to offshore foreign bank accounts
correct_answer_text: Social welfare and public benefit at affordable, subsidized rates
explanation: Activities in the private sector are guided by the motive to earn profits. The purpose of the public sector is not just to earn profits. Governments raise money through taxes and other ways to meet expenses on the services rendered by it for public welfare.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Why Government Must Invest in Heavy Infrastructure
question_text: Why does the public sector often undertake large infrastructure projects such as roads, railways, harbours and dams?
option_a: The private sector is constitutionally prohibited from using heavy machinery
option_b: Such projects can require very large investment, and charging the many users enough to recover the cost may be difficult; public provision can help make the facilities broadly available
option_c: Engineers refuse to work for private enterprises
option_d: Infrastructure has no effect on economic development
correct_answer_text: Such projects can require very large investment, and charging the many users enough to recover the cost may be difficult; public provision can help make the facilities broadly available
explanation: NCERT explains that some facilities require large spending and it may be difficult to collect sufficient payments from the many people who use them. Government investment can therefore help make important infrastructure available to the public. This does not mean private firms can never participate in infrastructure projects.

subject: Social Science
question_text: If all truck drivers and transport operators across India decide to go on a nationwide strike, what immediate economic consequence will follow?
option_a: The agricultural sector will automatically double its food grain output
option_b: Farmers will be unable to sell their vegetables and milk, causing produce to rot, while urban factories shut down due to lack of raw materials
option_c: Software companies will begin manufacturing heavy diesel trucks
option_d: Wholesale commodity prices in urban retail markets will drop to zero
correct_answer_text: Farmers will be unable to sell their vegetables and milk, causing produce to rot, while urban factories shut down due to lack of raw materials
explanation: This demonstrates sectoral interdependence: the tertiary sector (transport) links primary agricultural producers to urban consumers and secondary factory processors. Without transport, both primary and secondary sectors collapse.
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 2, Section 2.1 (Table on Interdependence)

subject: Social Science
question_text: A farmer cultivates raw cotton (Primary), a textile mill spins yarn and weaves cloth (Secondary), and a wholesale trader transports and markets the shirts to retail stores (Tertiary). This value chain proves that:
option_a: Raw cotton can be converted into shirts without any industrial processing
option_b: Wholesale traders belong exclusively to the primary agricultural sector
option_c: Secondary manufacturing can operate without raw materials from nature
option_d: Economic sectors do not function in isolation; each successive sector adds economic value to the output of preceding sectors
correct_answer_text: Economic sectors do not function in isolation; each successive sector adds economic value to the output of preceding sectors
explanation: Each stage in the supply chain builds upon the preceding stage: primary provides raw natural fibre, secondary transforms it into fabric and garments, and tertiary distributes it to the consumer.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Does disguised unemployment exist only in rural agriculture, or is it also visible in urban areas?
option_a: It is also visible in urban areas among thousands of casual street vendors, cart pushers, and repair persons who spend the whole day working but earn very little
option_b: It is strictly illegal and non-existent in urban municipalities
option_c: It only affects software engineers working in multinational corporate firms
option_d: It is legally restricted to government civil servants
correct_answer_text: It is also visible in urban areas among thousands of casual street vendors, cart pushers, and repair persons who spend the whole day working but earn very little
explanation: There are thousands of casual workers in the service sector in urban areas who search for daily employment (painters, plumbers, repair persons, street vendors). They may spend the whole day but earn very little; they do this work because they lack better opportunities.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In the historical 1977–78 to 2017–18 comparison presented by NCERT, industrial output rose by more than nine times while industrial employment rose around three times; service-sector production rose 14 times while employment rose around five times. What does this comparison establish?
option_a: Employment in industry and services grew faster than output
option_b: Output and employment in every sector grew at exactly the same rate
option_c: Production expanded much faster than employment in industry and services, showing that output growth did not translate into proportional job growth
option_d: The primary sector stopped employing workers by 2017–18
correct_answer_text: Production expanded much faster than employment in industry and services, showing that output growth did not translate into proportional job growth
explanation: The figures are historical comparisons cited in the 2026–27 NCERT chapter. They show that employment growth lagged behind production growth in the secondary and tertiary sectors. The comparison alone does not prove that every industry was capital-intensive or establish a current, economy-wide jobless-growth rate.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Potential of Tourism and Regional Crafts
question_text: What historical employment estimate does the 2026–27 NCERT chapter attribute to an earlier Planning Commission study on improving tourism?
option_a: More than 35 lakh additional jobs each year, as an estimate cited in the textbook
option_b: Exactly 500 jobs nationally over ten years
option_c: No additional jobs because tourism uses only unpaid labour
option_d: More than 100 crore jobs every six months
correct_answer_text: More than 35 lakh additional jobs each year, as an estimate cited in the textbook
explanation: The textbook reports an estimate from an earlier Planning Commission study that tourism improvement could provide additional employment to more than 35 lakh people each year. Treat this as a historical estimate quoted by NCERT, not a current forecast or verified present-day outcome.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Right to Education as Employment Generator
question_text: If public authorities expand access to schooling for children, what employment effect can follow from the need for additional educational facilities?
option_a: All adult workers would be forced into unemployment
option_b: Government revenues would immediately fall to zero
option_c: School textbook publishers would necessarily close
option_d: Additional jobs can be created for teachers, school administrators, construction workers and support staff
correct_answer_text: Additional jobs can be created for teachers, school administrators, construction workers and support staff
explanation: NCERT explains that bringing more children into educational institutions requires school buildings, teachers and other staff, which can generate employment. The Right to Education Act applies to children aged 6–14; the question therefore avoids incorrectly describing the wider school-age group as the Act's exact age coverage.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Credit as a Catalyst for Rural Employment
question_text: Why is the provision of cheap and affordable formal credit to small farmers considered a vital strategy for employment generation?
option_a: It allows farmers to permanently stop farming and move to luxury resorts
option_b: It forces commercial banks to forgive all corporate urban debts
option_c: It allows farmers to purchase seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation equipment without falling into the debt-trap of exploitative local moneylenders
option_d: It eliminates the need for agricultural harvests
correct_answer_text: It allows farmers to purchase seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation equipment without falling into the debt-trap of exploitative local moneylenders
explanation: Small farmers need credit for seeds, fertilizers, pumps, and pesticides. If local commercial or cooperative banks provide credit at reasonable interest, farmers can invest, grow multiple crops, and generate sustained on-farm employment.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Is the entire service sector in India expanding and prospering uniformly?
option_a: Yes; every service worker in India earns over ₹1,00,000 per month
option_b: No; only highly skilled services (IT, software, finance) are booming, while millions of unorganized service workers (hawkers, domestic maids, auto drivers) earn barely enough for survival
option_c: No; all software engineers in India are living below the national poverty line
option_d: Yes; there are no unorganized service workers left in Indian cities
correct_answer_text: No; only highly skilled services (IT, software, finance) are booming, while millions of unorganized service workers (hawkers, domestic maids, auto drivers) earn barely enough for survival
explanation: Service sector in India employs many different kinds of people. At one end there are a limited number of services that employ highly skilled and educated workers. At the other end, there are a very large number of workers engaged in services such as small shopkeepers, repair persons, transport persons. These people barely manage to earn a living.

subject: Social Science
question_text: According to the NCERT discussion of worker protection, what may some enterprises do when they operate outside or evade formal regulation?
option_a: They are required to provide every worker with a permanent government post
option_b: They are exempt from all taxation by an international treaty
option_c: They may evade taxes or labour-protection requirements, leaving workers with low, irregular and insecure employment
option_d: They must provide free imported raw materials to every worker
correct_answer_text: They may evade taxes or labour-protection requirements, leaving workers with low, irregular and insecure employment
explanation: NCERT notes that some enterprises adopt strategies to evade taxes and refuse to follow laws that protect labourers. The result can be low and irregular earnings, insecure jobs and lack of employment benefits. This is a description of the textbook's concern, not a claim that every unregistered enterprise behaves identically.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In India, what critical social reality intersects with employment in the unorganised sector?
option_a: A vast majority of workers in unorganised jobs belong to Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and backward communities, facing both economic insecurity and social discrimination
option_b: Unorganised workers belong exclusively to upper-caste royal dynasties
option_c: Caste has zero correlation with unorganised labour representation
option_d: Scheduled Castes are constitutionally barred from working in the unorganised sector
correct_answer_text: A vast majority of workers in unorganised jobs belong to Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and backward communities, facing both economic insecurity and social discrimination
explanation: A majority of workers from scheduled castes, tribes and backward communities find themselves in the unorganised sector. Besides getting the irregular and low-paid work, these workers also face social discrimination. Protection and support to the unorganised sector workers is thus necessary for both economic and social development.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Government Support: Electricity Subsidies for Farmers
question_text: Why may the government bear part of the cost of supplying electricity at affordable rates to small-scale producers and of procuring and distributing food grains through the public distribution system?
option_a: To guarantee profits to every private electricity company
option_b: To support small producers and help make essential food grains available to consumers at lower prices
option_c: To encourage wasteful use of water and electricity
option_d: To eliminate all private economic activity
correct_answer_text: To support small producers and help make essential food grains available to consumers at lower prices
explanation: NCERT gives two distinct examples of public support: affordable electricity can help small producers manage production costs, while procurement and sale through ration shops supports farmers and consumers. These measures serve different policy purposes; they should not be reduced to a single claim about market failure.

subject: Social Science
question_text: A farmer sells wheat to a flour mill for ₹10 per kg. The mill sells flour to a biscuit company for ₹12 per kg. The company sells four packets of biscuits to consumers for a total of ₹80. If the biscuits are the final goods, what value is counted as the final-goods contribution in this simplified example?
option_a: ₹102, by adding every intermediate sale to the final sale
option_b: ₹10, the value of wheat only
option_c: ₹22, the combined value of wheat and flour only
option_d: ₹80, the value of the final biscuits sold to consumers
correct_answer_text: ₹80, the value of the final biscuits sold to consumers
explanation: The ₹80 final-sale value already includes the value of intermediate inputs used to make the biscuits. Adding the wheat and flour transactions again would double-count those inputs. Strictly, this question asks for the final-goods value counted in the simplified example, not a complete value-added calculation for every producer.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In the fourth factor explaining tertiary growth in India, which new services have expanded with extraordinary speed over the last two decades?
option_a: Bullock cart freight and pigeon courier networks
option_b: Handloom spinning wheel workshops in urban centres
option_c: Coal-fired locomotive repair workshops
option_d: Information and communication technology (ICT) and business process outsourcing (BPO) services
correct_answer_text: Information and communication technology (ICT) and business process outsourcing (BPO) services
explanation: Over the past decade or so, certain new services such as those based on information and communication technology have become important and essential. The production of these services has been rising rapidly.

subject: Social Science
question_text: According to NCERT's historical comparison, why does the primary sector continue to employ a large share of India's workforce even though its contribution to total output is relatively smaller?
option_a: Because agricultural products have no market value
option_b: Because agriculture has no role in the Indian economy
option_c: Because insufficient alternative jobs have been created in the secondary and tertiary sectors, leaving surplus labour underemployed in agriculture
option_d: Because all agricultural workers are employed in permanent government posts
correct_answer_text: Because insufficient alternative jobs have been created in the secondary and tertiary sectors, leaving surplus labour underemployed in agriculture
explanation: NCERT explains that a similar shift in employment did not accompany the shift in production because not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors. As a result, many workers remain in agriculture, where some are underemployed. The textbook comparison is historical and should not be treated as a current labour-force estimate.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How can agro-processing units, cold-storage facilities and honey-collection centres in semi-rural areas help address underemployment?
option_a: By forcing rural workers to migrate to metropolitan cities
option_b: By replacing agricultural land with parking facilities
option_c: By creating local processing, storage, trade and service work and improving farmers' options for handling and marketing produce
option_d: By requiring all rural workers to become software programmers
correct_answer_text: By creating local processing, storage, trade and service work and improving farmers' options for handling and marketing produce
explanation: NCERT gives dal mills, cold storage and honey-collection centres as examples of activities that can create employment in or near rural areas. Storage may allow farmers to choose when to sell, but it does not guarantee a higher price or eliminate all intermediaries.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which of the following pairs represents classic examples of the Indian Public Sector?
option_a: Indian Railways and Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL)
option_b: Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS)
option_c: Infosys Technologies and Mahindra & Mahindra
option_d: Adani Ports and Larsen & Toubro (L&T)
correct_answer_text: Indian Railways and Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL)
explanation: Indian Railways and Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) are owned, financed, and operated by the Government of India for public service and national infrastructure.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which of the following pairs represents classic enterprises operating in the Private Sector in India?
option_a: Indian Post Office and Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL)
option_b: Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Coal India Limited (CIL)
option_c: Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) and Reliance Industries Limited (RIL)
option_d: National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) and Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
correct_answer_text: Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) and Reliance Industries Limited (RIL)
explanation: TISCO (Tata Steel) and Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) are privately owned corporations managed by shareholders and boards of directors for commercial profitability.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Current Rural Employment Guarantee: Productive Public Works
question_text: Which type of public works is consistent with the rural asset-creation and natural-resource priorities of the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025?
option_a: Building five-star luxury hotels for private landlords
option_b: Water conservation, restoration of local water bodies, drought resilience and rural connectivity works
option_c: Assembling consumer electronics for private export
option_d: Constructing private swimming pools for urban households
correct_answer_text: Water conservation, restoration of local water bodies, drought resilience and rural connectivity works
explanation: The VB-G RAM G framework links wage employment with durable rural assets and resilient development. Water conservation and rural infrastructure are consistent with these purposes. This question concerns the current 2025 Act, not the repealed MGNREGA 2005 framework.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why are public regulation and social-protection measures important for workers in the unorganised sector?
option_a: Because workers in unorganised employment may face irregular earnings, weak job security, unsafe conditions and limited access to employment benefits
option_b: Because all unorganised workers are employed by foreign governments
option_c: Because unorganised workers are exempt from ordinary consumer markets
option_d: Because every unorganised enterprise is legally owned by the state
correct_answer_text: Because workers in unorganised employment may face irregular earnings, weak job security, unsafe conditions and limited access to employment benefits
explanation: NCERT describes many unorganised-sector jobs as low-paid, irregular and insecure, with limited provision for overtime, paid leave or sickness benefits. Effective regulation and social-protection measures can help address these vulnerabilities. Conditions vary across occupations and employers.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How does India's sectoral transition differ fundamentally from the classical path followed by advanced industrialized nations like Britain and the USA?
option_a: India industrialized completely before developing any primary agricultural sector
option_b: India has never developed any service or transport infrastructure
option_c: India has 90% of its workforce employed in heavy steel foundries
option_d: India leapfrogged directly from an agrarian economy to a service-dominant GDP economy without the manufacturing sector ever becoming the principal employer of labour
correct_answer_text: India leapfrogged directly from an agrarian economy to a service-dominant GDP economy without the manufacturing sector ever becoming the principal employer of labour
explanation: Unlike Western economies where surplus agrarian workers shifted first to factory manufacturing, India's secondary sector generated relatively few jobs; the GDP shift bypassed secondary dominance straight into services, leaving surplus labour stranded in agriculture.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: A-R: Counting Final Goods in GDP
question_text:
Assertion (A): While computing the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), only the value of final goods and services is considered.
Reason (R): Intermediate goods are completely consumed during the production process and their monetary value is already reflected in the market price of the final good.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Intermediate goods like flour and sugar are absorbed into final goods like biscuits; counting intermediate goods separately would cause the error of double counting.

subject: Social Science
question_text:
Assertion (A): Disguised unemployment exists extensively in the Indian agricultural sector.
Reason (R): More people are engaged in farming activities than strictly required, and withdrawing a portion of farmworkers does not cause any decline in total agricultural output.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Surplus farm labourers share work on family plots; their marginal productivity is zero because pulling them away to other jobs leaves crop production unaffected.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: A-R: Rising Dominance of Tertiary Sector
question_text: According to the historical comparison in NCERT, which sector had become India's largest producing sector by 2017–18?
option_a: The tertiary (service) sector
option_b: The primary (agricultural) sector
option_c: The secondary (industrial) sector
option_d: All three sectors had equal production
correct_answer_text: The tertiary (service) sector
explanation: NCERT's historical data for 2017–18 show that the tertiary sector became the largest producing sector, replacing the primary sector. The textbook also discusses several reasons for service-sector growth, including basic services, demand linked to agriculture and industry, rising incomes and information technology.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: A-R: VB-G RAM G Act as Right to Work
question_text:
Assertion (A): The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 provides a statutory rural wage-employment guarantee and is described in the NCERT chapter in the context of the 'Right to Work'.
Reason (R): Under the Act, a covered rural household is entitled to a statutory guarantee of not less than 125 days of wage employment in a financial year, and an eligible applicant may become entitled to unemployment allowance if work is not provided within the prescribed 15-day period, subject to the Act and State Scheme.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 replaced MGNREGA 2005 and provides a guarantee of not less than 125 days of wage employment per covered rural household. Section 11 provides for unemployment allowance where work is not provided within the statutory period, subject to the Act and applicable State Scheme. The Act provides for commencement by a separate Central Government notification.

subject: Social Science
question_text:
Assertion (A): Workers in the organised sector generally have greater employment security than workers in the unorganised sector.
Reason (R): Organised enterprises are registered and their employment conditions are subject to applicable rules and labour laws.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: NCERT describes organised-sector workplaces as registered and subject to rules and regulations, with more regular terms of employment and greater security. The exact protections depend on the applicable law, establishment and employment arrangement; registration alone does not guarantee identical benefits to every worker.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: A-R: Need for Public Sector in Infrastructure
question_text:
Assertion (A): The public sector has an important role in providing large-scale infrastructure such as roads, railways, harbours and irrigation dams.
Reason (R): Such facilities can require very large investment, and collecting payments from all users may be difficult or may make the service unaffordable if costs are fully passed on.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: NCERT explains that roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity generation and irrigation dams may require heavy spending, and it may be difficult to collect money from all users. Public investment helps ensure that these facilities are available more broadly. Private participation is not ruled out.

subject: Social Science
question_text:
Assertion (A): India's shift in production towards the tertiary sector has not been matched by an equally large shift of employment out of agriculture in the historical comparison discussed by NCERT.
Reason (R): Not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors to absorb the workers who were underemployed in agriculture.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: NCERT attributes the limited shift in employment to insufficient job creation in the secondary and tertiary sectors. Its output and employment comparisons are historical textbook data; they do not by themselves establish that all sectoral growth was capital- or technology-intensive.

subject: Social Science
question_text:
Assertion (A): The primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors are deeply interdependent.
Reason (R): An increase in agricultural output increases the demand for industrial processing and requires tertiary transport, banking, and storage services.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: No sector functions autonomously: primary supplies raw materials to secondary, secondary supplies machines/fertilizers to primary, and tertiary provides transport/finance to both.

subject: Social Science
question_text:
Assertion (A): Informalisation of employment can occur when organised enterprises outsource work to contractors or rely more heavily on temporary and contractual labour.
Reason (R): Some enterprises use subcontracting and contractual hiring to reduce labour costs and avoid or limit obligations associated with direct, permanent employment.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Outsourcing and contractual hiring can make employment less secure even when work is performed within the supply chain of an organised enterprise. It is more precise to describe this as informalisation of employment than to say that workers automatically move from an organised enterprise into the unorganised sector; the legal classification depends on the employer and employment arrangement.

subject: Social Science
question_text:
Assertion (A): Affordable rural credit can help create non-farm employment when it is used to establish or expand rural enterprises.
Reason (R): Access to lower-cost loans can help households invest in activities such as small agro-processing units, flour mills and other rural businesses.
option_a: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
option_b: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
option_c: (A) is true, but (R) is false.
option_d: (A) is false, but (R) is true.
correct_answer_text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Affordable credit can support non-farm employment when it finances small rural enterprises and agro-processing. Investment in irrigation or livestock may strengthen farm or allied-sector livelihoods, but does not automatically create non-farm employment.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Laxmi's family has 5 members working on their two-hectare unirrigated plot, producing 15 quintals of jowar. When an NGO helps two members secure jobs in a nearby spinning mill, the remaining three members still produce 15 quintals of jowar. What does this confirm?
option_a: The two workers were previously underemployed (disguisedly unemployed), and their removal caused zero loss of agricultural output
option_b: The plot has become three times more fertile due to soil erosion
option_c: Laxmi's family has abandoned agriculture completely
option_d: The spinning mill operates as an unorganised enterprise
correct_answer_text: The two workers were previously underemployed (disguisedly unemployed), and their removal caused zero loss of agricultural output
explanation: Because production remained at 15 quintals even after two workers left, those workers were contributing zero marginal product — the textbook definition of disguised unemployment.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Analysis: Kanta in the Organised Sector
question_text: Kanta works in an office from 9:30 AM to 5:30 PM, receives a regular monthly salary via direct bank transfer, gets medical benefits, paid Sunday holidays, and provident fund contributions. This case shows that Kanta:
option_a: Works in an unorganised agricultural farm
option_b: Enjoys the legal protections, job security, and statutory social welfare benefits guaranteed in the Organised Sector
option_c: Is vulnerable to immediate dismissal without notice on Monday morning
option_d: Is self-employed in the informal cottage sector
correct_answer_text: Enjoys the legal protections, job security, and statutory social welfare benefits guaranteed in the Organised Sector
explanation: Kanta's terms of employment demonstrate all criteria of the organised sector: formal appointment, fixed hours, paid leaves, medical care, and retirement provident fund.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Analysis: Kamal in the Unorganised Sector
question_text: Kamal is a daily-wage assistant in a grocery shop. He works long hours, receives no paid sick leave, has no appointment letter and may be asked to leave when business slows. Which feature of employment does this example illustrate?
option_a: That Kamal necessarily earns more than a regular salaried worker
option_b: That all grocery shops are part of the public sector
option_c: Insecure and irregular work with limited employment benefits, commonly associated with unorganised employment
option_d: That Kamal is a permanent civil-service employee
correct_answer_text: Insecure and irregular work with limited employment benefits, commonly associated with unorganised employment
explanation: The example reflects the features described by NCERT for unorganised employment: irregular work, lack of paid leave and limited job security. The facts given do not establish whether Kamal is paid below the applicable minimum wage, so the answer does not make that additional claim.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Analysis: VB-G RAM G Rural Asset Creation
question_text: In a drought-prone village, 80 eligible rural workers are engaged in a water-conservation project under the VB-G RAM G framework. Which pair of outcomes best describes the purpose of such work?
option_a: Draining groundwater to create private resorts
option_b: Forcing all villagers to leave agriculture permanently
option_c: Eliminating the need for future irrigation
option_d: Providing wage employment within the household-based statutory guarantee while creating a durable water-conservation asset
correct_answer_text: Providing wage employment within the household-based statutory guarantee while creating a durable water-conservation asset
explanation: The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 provides a guarantee of not less than 125 days of wage employment per covered rural household, subject to statutory conditions. Its framework also links employment to durable rural assets, including works supporting water conservation and resilience. The guarantee is not 125 days for each individual worker.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Case Analysis: Biscuit Production Supply Chain
question_text: A packet of biscuits is manufactured using flour, sugar, vegetable oil, and packaging paper. In computing national income, why is the statistician instructed to include only the retail price of the biscuit packet?
option_a: Because agricultural wheat has no monetary value until it reaches the consumer
option_b: Because counting the separate sales of wheat, flour, sugar, and oil before the biscuit is sold would count the same value multiple times, artificially inflating GDP
option_c: Because biscuit manufacturers do not pay income taxes to the government
option_d: Because intermediate goods are not traded in market economies
correct_answer_text: Because counting the separate sales of wheat, flour, sugar, and oil before the biscuit is sold would count the same value multiple times, artificially inflating GDP
explanation: Intermediate values are completely absorbed within the final product. Counting both intermediate inputs and final goods creates the classic GDP error of double counting.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Construction workers gathering at urban labour chowks each morning to seek daily work illustrate which employment reality?
option_a: Permanent tenured employment in the public sector
option_b: Regular organised-sector employment with assured monthly salaries
option_c: Software consultancy employment in IT parks
option_d: Precarious daily-wage work where hiring and earnings depend on daily demand and workers may lack regular employment benefits
correct_answer_text: Precarious daily-wage work where hiring and earnings depend on daily demand and workers may lack regular employment benefits
explanation: Daily hiring at labour chowks illustrates irregular and insecure work. The example does not establish that every worker lacks every form of safety equipment or statutory compensation; actual protections depend on the applicable law and employment arrangement.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Government Support for Small Scale Industries
question_text: Why does the central government provide marketing support, subsidized raw materials, and institutional credit to small scale industries (SSIs)?
option_a: Because small scale industries are highly labour-intensive and generate substantial manufacturing employment across tier-2 and tier-3 towns
option_b: Because small scale industries produce heavy nuclear submarines
option_c: Because small scale industries are owned exclusively by state governments
option_d: Because multinational corporations refuse to sell consumer goods
correct_answer_text: Because small scale industries are highly labour-intensive and generate substantial manufacturing employment across tier-2 and tier-3 towns
explanation: Small-scale industries are crucial for decentralized industrialization and employment generation because they absorb more labour per unit of capital than large mega-factories.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which of the following factors best explains why the expansion of agriculture and industry directly accelerates tertiary service growth?
option_a: Agriculture and industry destroy service sector employment
option_b: Farmers stop buying clothes once crop harvests increase
option_c: Greater farm and factory production requires more transport trucks, commercial warehouses, banking credit, and marketing retail distribution
option_d: Factory workers refuse to use commercial transport networks
correct_answer_text: Greater farm and factory production requires more transport trucks, commercial warehouses, banking credit, and marketing retail distribution
explanation: The development of agriculture and industry leads to the development of services such as transport, trade, and storage. The greater the development of primary and secondary sectors, the greater the demand for such services.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Public Sector Health and Education Obligations
question_text: Why does NCERT identify the provision of quality basic education and healthcare as an important responsibility of the government?
option_a: Because private hospitals are legally barred from treating patients
option_b: Because private schools are constitutionally prohibited
option_c: Because the government must help ensure access to essential services and human development, including for people who may not be able to afford adequate provision privately
option_d: Because all private providers are prohibited from charging fees
correct_answer_text: Because the government must help ensure access to essential services and human development, including for people who may not be able to afford adequate provision privately
explanation: NCERT emphasises the government's responsibility to provide health and education facilities for all and to address wider human-development needs such as safe drinking water, housing, food and nutrition. Private providers may also operate; public responsibility is to help ensure broad and equitable access.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Synthesis: Policy Blueprint for Sectoral Health
question_text: To achieve balanced, inclusive, and employment-rich economic growth, which integrated strategy must India execute across its sectors?
option_a: Shut down all primary agricultural farming and import all food grains from abroad
option_b: Nationalize all private corporate software companies and dismantle private enterprises
option_c: Abolish all labour welfare laws to eliminate the organised sector completely
option_d: Modernize agriculture and agro-processing, stimulate labour-intensive manufacturing, expand affordable credit and skill development, and formalize unorganised worker protections
correct_answer_text: Modernize agriculture and agro-processing, stimulate labour-intensive manufacturing, expand affordable credit and skill development, and formalize unorganised worker protections
explanation: Sustainable development requires agricultural productivity gains, expanding job-rich manufacturing, formalizing unorganised workers, and providing universal public health and education.
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 2, Chapter Summary

subject: Social Science
question_text: In a barter economy where goods are directly exchanged without the use of money, which essential condition must be satisfied?
option_a: Double coincidence of wants (both parties must agree to sell and buy each other's commodities)
option_b: A formal promissory guarantee certified by the village panchayat
option_c: Gold coins deposited with an escrow magistrate
option_d: A fixed exchange price list published by the state government
correct_answer_text: Double coincidence of wants (both parties must agree to sell and buy each other's commodities)
explanation: In an ancient barter economy where commodities are exchanged directly without any monetary medium, exchange is constrained by the 'double coincidence of wants'. This means that what one party desires to sell must coincide precisely with what the other party wishes to buy (e.g. a shoemaker needing wheat must find a wheat farmer wanting shoes). Because searching for matching reciprocal trading partners is exceedingly difficult, time-consuming, and inefficient, the introduction of money revolutionized commerce by eliminating this obstacle.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why is money referred to as a 'medium of exchange'?
option_a: Because it is minted exclusively from precious silver and gold bullion
option_b: Because it acts as an intermediary instrument in the transactions and exchange of goods and services
option_c: Because it can only be exchanged inside foreign diplomatic embassies
option_d: Because it changes its face value automatically every month
correct_answer_text: Because it acts as an intermediary instrument in the transactions and exchange of goods and services
explanation: Money is termed a 'medium of exchange' because it acts as a universally accepted intermediary asset in the purchase and sale of goods, assets, and services. In a modern economy, a person holding money does not have to search for double coincidences; they can immediately purchase any commodity or service desired from any merchant. By decoupling the act of sale from the act of purchase, money solves the indivisibility and storage problems of barter, serving as a universal standard unit of account and store of economic value.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Unlike historical money (such as grain, cattle, gold, and silver coins), modern Indian currency:
option_a: Can be eaten as nutritious food during famines
option_b: Is valid only within 5 kilometers of the Reserve Bank headquarters
option_c: Must be redeemed for silver bullion at the post office every year
option_d: Is not made of precious metal and has virtually no intrinsic everyday value of its own
correct_answer_text: Is not made of precious metal and has virtually no intrinsic everyday value of its own
explanation: NCERT contrasts modern currency with earlier commodity forms such as grain, cattle and precious-metal coins. Modern notes and coins are not made of precious metal and have no everyday use of their own; they are accepted because currency is authorised by the government. Avoid treating the textbook wording as a claim that every modern payment instrument is legal tender.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In India, which institution has the sole right to issue banknotes under Section 22 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (noting that the ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India)?
option_a: The State Bank of India (SBI)
option_b: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
option_c: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
option_d: The Ministry of Heavy Industries
correct_answer_text: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
explanation: Section 22 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 gives the RBI the sole right to issue banknotes in India. The ₹1 note is an important exception: it is issued by the Government of India. The question refers to RBI-issued banknotes, not every denomination of currency. RBI's currency FAQ explains the respective roles of RBI and the Government of India.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why is the Indian rupee widely accepted for settling monetary obligations in India?
option_a: Because bank notes contain microchips tracked by police satellites
option_b: Because the law legalizes the use of Rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India
option_c: Because merchants are paid a commission by the World Bank on every note
option_d: Because all shopkeepers are government civil service employees
correct_answer_text: Because the law legalizes the use of Rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India
explanation: NCERT explains that the law legalises the use of the rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions. For legal precision, legal-tender status is subject to the applicable statutory provisions: banknotes issued by RBI (unless withdrawn) are legal tender, while coins have denomination-specific limits under the Coinage Act, 2011. The RBI's currency FAQ sets out these limits.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why are deposits in bank savings or current accounts referred to as 'Demand Deposits'?
option_a: Because the government demands 90% of the deposit as income tax
option_b: Because the depositor must file an application in court before withdrawing money
option_c: Because the deposited money can be withdrawn by the depositor on demand at any time
option_d: Because banks demand that depositors keep gold bullion in their lockers
correct_answer_text: Because the deposited money can be withdrawn by the depositor on demand at any time
explanation: Individuals and commercial businesses deposit surplus cash into bank accounts for safety and to earn interest. Because the funds held in savings and current bank accounts can be withdrawn or transferred by the account holder 'on demand' at any time—via bank branch cash counters, ATMs, cheques, or electronic fund transfers (NEFT/RTGS/UPI)—these deposits are technically classified as 'Demand Deposits'. Demand deposits share the essential characteristics of cash, functioning as a primary component of the modern money supply.

subject: Social Science
question_text: A cheque is best defined as:
option_a: A government tax receipt confirming property ownership
option_b: A currency note printed by commercial private banks
option_c: A postal telegram ordering delivery of agricultural goods
option_d: A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the drawer's account to the person in whose name the cheque has been issued
correct_answer_text: A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the drawer's account to the person in whose name the cheque has been issued
explanation: A cheque is a negotiable banking instrument in paper form instructing a bank to pay a specific sum of money from the account of the person writing the cheque (the drawer) to the person, business, or entity in whose name the instrument has been drawn (the payee). Cheques allow large financial transactions, business trade settlements, and debt clearances to occur seamlessly between bank accounts without the physical handling, transport, or risk of carrying bulky paper banknotes (NCERT Class 10 Economics Chapter 3).

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Banks’ Cash Holdings in the NCERT Illustration
question_text: In the NCERT textbook illustration of bank lending, approximately what proportion of deposits do banks keep as cash to meet depositors’ day-to-day withdrawal needs?
option_a: About 5% of their deposits, as described in the textbook illustration
option_b: 100% of their deposits
option_c: Less than 0.1% of their deposits
option_d: Exactly 75% of their deposits
correct_answer_text: About 5% of their deposits, as described in the textbook illustration
explanation: The NCERT chapter gives about 5% as an illustrative share of deposits that banks keep as cash to meet withdrawals. This is a textbook illustration, not the current statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR). CRR is a separate regulatory requirement involving balances maintained by banks with the RBI; it should not be described as cash held in bank branches or vaults.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Main Source of Income for Commercial Banks
question_text: What constitutes the primary source of income for commercial banks?
option_a: Monetary grants received every month from the United Nations
option_b: Profits earned from selling real estate properties
option_c: The difference between the higher interest rate charged on loans to borrowers and the lower interest rate paid to depositors
option_d: Municipal fees collected from printing currency notes
correct_answer_text: The difference between the higher interest rate charged on loans to borrowers and the lower interest rate paid to depositors
explanation: Commercial banks act as financial intermediaries between depositors who have surplus funds and borrowers who require credit for investment. Banks pay a modest interest rate to depositors on their savings and fixed deposits (e.g. 4%–6% per annum). Simultaneously, banks lend these deposited funds to borrowers at a significantly higher interest rate (e.g. 9%–14% per annum). The financial spread—the difference between the interest charged on loans and the interest paid to depositors—constitutes the primary operating income of banks.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In the NCERT case of Salim, a shoe manufacturer receiving a festival order for 3,000 pairs of shoes, how did credit impact his business?
option_a: It enabled him to procure raw materials, hire extra workers, fulfill the contract on time, earn good profits, and repay the loan
option_b: It forced him to sell his family ancestral home and become a landless labourer
option_c: It resulted in criminal prosecution and bankruptcy
option_d: It caused him to abandon leather shoe manufacturing completely
correct_answer_text: It enabled him to procure raw materials, hire extra workers, fulfill the contract on time, earn good profits, and repay the loan
explanation: In NCERT’s example, Salim uses credit to meet working-capital needs: he obtains leather on credit and an advance from the trader, completes the 3,000-pair order, earns a good profit and repays the amounts borrowed. This is an example of credit playing a positive role by supporting production and increasing earnings.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In the case of Swapna, a small farmer who took a loan for groundnut cultivation and suffered crop failure due to pests, credit resulted in:
option_a: Instant wealth making her the largest landowner in the village
option_b: Complete debt forgiveness granted by the World Bank
option_c: Starting a successful multinational pesticide corporation
option_d: A debt-trap where she had to sell a portion of her land to repay the loan
correct_answer_text: A debt-trap where she had to sell a portion of her land to repay the loan
explanation: Collateral is a tangible physical or financial asset owned by the borrower—such as agricultural land, a house, commercial property, vehicle, gold jewellery, or fixed deposits with banks—that the borrower pledges to the lender as a security guarantee for a loan. If the borrower defaults and fails to repay the credit, the lender has the legal right to repossess and liquidate the pledged collateral to recover the unpaid principal and accrued interest. Pledging collateral mitigates the lender's credit default risk.

subject: Social Science
question_text: 'Collateral' in a loan agreement is defined as:
option_a: A cash bribe paid to the bank manager to approve the loan application
option_b: An asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestock, bank deposits) and pledges to the lender as a guarantee until the loan is repaid
option_c: A certificate of good conduct issued by the local member of parliament
option_d: An insurance policy against foreign currency fluctuations
correct_answer_text: An asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestock, bank deposits) and pledges to the lender as a guarantee until the loan is repaid
explanation: Every formal or informal loan agreement is governed by the 'terms of credit', which specify four mandatory components: (1) The specific interest rate charged on the principal amount; (2) Collateral security required to guarantee the loan; (3) Documentation requirements verifying the borrower's identity, income, and employment; (4) The mode of repayment (e.g. monthly EMIs, bullet lump-sum, cash or bank transfer). The terms of credit vary widely depending on the nature of the lender and the creditworthiness of the borrower.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which four components together constitute the 'Terms of Credit' in any formal lending transaction?
option_a: Political party membership, caste certificate, passport, and driving license
option_b: Interest rate, collateral, documentation required, and mode of repayment
option_c: Gold jewellery, silver coins, foreign currency, and postal stamps
option_d: Tax audit reports, company balance sheet, factory blueprint, and electricity bill
correct_answer_text: Interest rate, collateral, documentation required, and mode of repayment
explanation: In India, credit is bifurcated into two sectors: (1) Formal sector: Commercial banks and cooperatives regulated by the RBI, which charge fair, regulated interest rates (usually 8% to 12% per year) but require collateral and strict documentation; (2) Informal sector: Village moneylenders, traders, and relatives who demand no asset collateral or paperwork, but charge usurious interest rates (often 36% to 60%+ annually) and frequently deploy exploitative or coercive recovery practices, trapping poor rural families in chronic poverty.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Which of the following lenders belong strictly to the 'Formal Sector' of credit in India?
option_a: Village moneylenders and agricultural traders
option_b: Friends, neighbours, and relatives
option_c: Employers and local commission agents
option_d: Commercial Banks and Cooperative Societies
correct_answer_text: Commercial Banks and Cooperative Societies
explanation: The formal credit sector in India comprises institutional lending entities that are registered with and supervised by the government, primarily commercial banks (public sector banks like SBI, private banks) and rural cooperative credit societies. In contrast, the informal credit sector consists of unorganized, unregulated lenders: local village moneylenders, agricultural commission agents, traders, landlords, employers, and personal friends or relatives, which operate outside the regulatory oversight of the Reserve Bank of India.

subject: Social Science
question_text: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans. Which of the following is a key objective of this supervision?
option_a: Ordering banks to charge a 50% interest rate on rural agricultural loans
option_b: Forbidding banks from keeping any liquid cash reserves in their vaults
option_c: Ensuring that banks give loans not only to profit-making businesses and rich traders, but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries, and small borrowers
option_d: Prohibiting commercial banks from opening branches in rural areas
correct_answer_text: Ensuring that banks give loans not only to profit-making businesses and rich traders, but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries, and small borrowers
explanation: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) exercises statutory supervision over the formal banking sector to achieve multiple policy objectives: (1) Ensuring that banks actually maintain minimum cash reserve ratios; (2) Monitoring loan allocations through mandatory Priority Sector Lending (PSL) targets, ensuring commercial credit flows to small farmers, rural artisans, and small-scale entrepreneurs rather than flowing exclusively to wealthy corporate conglomerates; (3) Regulating transparent interest rates and capital adequacy norms.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why is borrowing from the informal credit sector (moneylenders) frequently disastrous for poor rural households?
option_a: There is no supervisory organization, interest rates are exorbitantly high (often 3% to 5% per month), and lenders use coercive recovery methods
option_b: Moneylenders require three government identity cards and a university diploma
option_c: Informal loans must be repaid in British Pounds Sterling
option_d: Moneylenders are legally barred from lending cash to farmers
correct_answer_text: There is no supervisory organization, interest rates are exorbitantly high (often 3% to 5% per month), and lenders use coercive recovery methods
explanation: Borrowing from informal moneylenders is frequently devastating for vulnerable households because: (1) There is no regulatory agency overseeing informal credit activities or capping usurious interest rates (which can reach 60% per year); (2) High borrowing costs consume most of the debtor's agricultural income, leaving little for subsistence; (3) Informal lenders frequently deploy manipulative record-keeping, harassment, and coercive seizure of land and livestock to enforce repayment, cementing generational bonded indebtedness.

subject: Social Science
question_text: According to official data presented in NCERT (Graph 2), what percentage of loans taken by poor households in urban areas comes from informal sources?
option_a: 46% of their loans come from formal sources
option_b: Zero percent, because all poor households use nationalized banks
option_c: Exactly 50% comes from informal sources
option_d: 54% of their loans come from informal sources
correct_answer_text: 54% of their loans come from informal sources
explanation: NCERT Graph 2 reports that 54% of loans taken by poor urban households are from informal sources and 46% from formal sources. For rich urban households, the corresponding informal share is 17% and formal share is 83%. These are the textbook’s survey figures, not current live estimates.
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, Graph 2

subject: Social Science
question_text: A typical Self-Help Group (SHG) organized in rural India consists of how many members, meeting and pooling their savings regularly?
option_a: 15 to 20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood
option_b: 500 to 1,000 members from different districts
option_c: Only 2 members (a husband and wife)
option_d: Exactly 100 registered company directors
correct_answer_text: 15 to 20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood
explanation: A standard Self-Help Group (SHG) organized in rural India consists of 15 to 20 members, usually women belonging to one local village neighbourhood, who meet and pool their savings on a regular weekly or monthly basis. Individual savings typically range from ₹25 to ₹100 or more per meeting, depending on members' economic capacity. Members can take small, low-interest loans from the group's pooled corpus to meet immediate family needs (such as medical treatment, seeds, or school fees) without falling prey to village moneylenders.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How do Self-Help Groups solve the problem of 'lack of collateral' for rural poor women seeking bank loans?
option_a: The members mortgage their ancestral village farmland to foreign investors
option_b: The panchayat sarpanch signs a blank cheque on behalf of the group
option_c: After regular savings for a year or two, the group becomes eligible for bank loans sanctioned in the name of the group without requiring individual asset collateral
option_d: The Reserve Bank directly deposits ₹10 lakh into each member's personal account
correct_answer_text: After regular savings for a year or two, the group becomes eligible for bank loans sanctioned in the name of the group without requiring individual asset collateral
explanation: The greatest structural hurdle preventing rural poor women from securing formal bank loans is the complete absence of physical asset collateral. Self-Help Groups (SHGs) resolve this impasse through collective social guarantee: when an SHG maintains disciplined savings and financial records for one to two years, commercial banks sanction microcredit directly in the collective name of the group without requiring individual collateral. All members are jointly responsible for timely repayment, guaranteeing high recovery rates.

subject: Social Science
question_text: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, which successfully pioneered micro-credit for millions of poor women, was founded by Nobel Peace laureate:
option_a: Amartya Sen
option_b: Professor Muhammad Yunus
option_c: Manmohan Singh
option_d: Abhijit Banerjee
correct_answer_text: Professor Muhammad Yunus
explanation: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh was founded in the 1970s by economist Professor Muhammad Yunus, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006 for pioneering micro-credit and micro-finance. Starting as a modest research project, Grameen Bank demonstrated that even the poorest rural women, possessing zero physical collateral, are highly creditworthy and reliable entrepreneurs when organized into micro-credit circles. By 2018, Grameen Bank served over 9 million low-income borrowers across 81,600 villages throughout Bangladesh.

subject: Social Science
question_text: A shoe manufacturer wants to sell shoes and buy wheat. In a barter system without money, what difficulty does he immediately encounter?
option_a: He must obtain an export license from the United Nations
option_b: He must find a wheat-growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat, but also wants to buy the exact size and style of shoes he makes
option_c: He is legally prohibited from consuming wheat products
option_d: He can only trade with merchants who speak foreign languages
correct_answer_text: He must find a wheat-growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat, but also wants to buy the exact size and style of shoes he makes
explanation: Both parties have to agree to sell and buy each other's commodities. If the farmer wants clothes instead of shoes, no exchange can occur — the classic obstacle of double coincidence of wants.

subject: Social Science
question_text: What would happen to a commercial bank if all of its depositors arrive on the exact same morning demanding to withdraw their entire savings in cash?
option_a: The bank would immediately double its profits by collecting withdrawal fees
option_b: The bank would print new paper currency in its back office within ten minutes
option_c: The bank would face a liquidity crisis ('bank run') and be unable to pay all depositors immediately because most funds are tied up in long-term loans
option_d: The bank manager would be declared the permanent governor of the Reserve Bank
correct_answer_text: The bank would face a liquidity crisis ('bank run') and be unable to pay all depositors immediately because most funds are tied up in long-term loans
explanation: Banks keep only a small proportion of deposits as cash and use a major portion to extend loans. If all depositors demanded their entire balances at the same time, the bank could be unable to meet all withdrawals immediately because much of the deposited money has been lent out. This is a liquidity problem; it does not by itself establish that the bank is insolvent.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why can credit for agricultural crop production expose borrowers to significant risks?
option_a: Because crop yields can be affected by factors such as rainfall, pests and other conditions, reducing the income available for repayment
option_b: Because farmers are legally prohibited from borrowing from banks
option_c: Because agricultural loans never require repayment
option_d: Because crop production always earns less than manufacturing
correct_answer_text: Because crop yields can be affected by factors such as rainfall, pests and other conditions, reducing the income available for repayment
explanation: Crop production involves considerable input costs, and repayment is often dependent on income from the harvest. Pests or adverse weather can reduce or destroy the crop, making repayment difficult. NCERT uses Swapna’s case to show how credit can worsen a borrower’s position when a crop fails; this does not mean every agricultural loan is destructive.

subject: Social Science
question_text: What is meant by the economic term 'debt-trap'?
option_a: A government tax audit conducted on private commercial companies
option_b: An automated machine that detects counterfeit currency notes
option_c: A legal contract restricting a worker from changing employers
option_d: A situation where credit pushes the borrower into a financial crisis from which recovery is impossible without selling productive assets or taking further debt
correct_answer_text: A situation where credit pushes the borrower into a financial crisis from which recovery is impossible without selling productive assets or taking further debt
explanation: A debt-trap occurs when repayment of a loan requires taking another loan or selling productive assets (like land). Instead of improving the borrower's earnings, credit leaves them worse off and trapped in compounding debt.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why do commercial banks insist on collateral before sanctioning a housing loan or vehicle loan?
option_a: To confiscate all borrower belongings regardless of whether loan is repaid
option_b: To transfer ownership of the property to the Reserve Bank of India
option_c: To prevent borrowers from ever entering the bank branch premises
option_d: To serve as a security against default, allowing the bank to sell the property to recover the unpaid loan amount if the borrower fails to repay
correct_answer_text: To serve as a security against default, allowing the bank to sell the property to recover the unpaid loan amount if the borrower fails to repay
explanation: Collateral protects the lender against default. If the borrower defaults, the lender has the legal right to sell the pledged asset to recover the outstanding principal and interest.

subject: Social Science
question_text: In NCERT’s Sonpur example, why does Shyamal use credit from an agricultural trader for cultivation?
option_a: The trader supplies farm inputs on credit and the farmer promises to sell the crop to the trader when it is ready
option_b: Because formal banks are legally prohibited from lending to farmers
option_c: Because informal loans are always cheaper than bank loans
option_d: Because farmers are required by law to borrow from local traders
correct_answer_text: The trader supplies farm inputs on credit and the farmer promises to sell the crop to the trader when it is ready
explanation: In the NCERT Sonpur example, Shyamal receives farm inputs on credit from an agricultural trader and promises to sell the crop to that trader. The arrangement helps him obtain inputs, but the tied sale can allow the trader to buy the crop at a low price and resell it later. This is a specific fieldwork example, not a universal explanation for all small farmers.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Agricultural Trader as Lender: Tied Credit
question_text: In the NCERT fieldwork in Sonpur village, farmer Shyamal obtains crop inputs on credit from an agricultural trader. What condition is linked to this credit arrangement?
option_a: The farmer promises to sell the crop to the trader when it is ready, allowing the trader to buy low and sell later when prices rise
option_b: The farmer transfers ownership of his land to the trader immediately
option_c: The farmer must repay the loan in foreign currency
option_d: The farmer agrees to stop cultivating potatoes permanently
correct_answer_text: The farmer promises to sell the crop to the trader when it is ready, allowing the trader to buy low and sell later when prices rise
explanation: In NCERT, Shyamal borrows from an agricultural trader who supplies farm inputs on credit. Shyamal promises to sell the crop to the trader. The textbook explains that this can benefit the trader by enabling a low-price purchase and later resale when market prices rise; it does not specify a formally fixed price in advance.
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 3, Section 3.3 (Fieldwork in Sonpur)

subject: Social Science
question_text: How do Agricultural Cooperative Societies (like Krishak Cooperative in Sonpur) raise funds to lend to their farmer members?
option_a: They sell foreign treasury bills on international currency exchanges
option_b: They collect mandatory taxes from urban shopping malls
option_c: They pool deposits from member farmers, use those deposits as collateral to obtain a large loan from a bank, and then lend to members for seeds, implements, and tube wells
option_d: They print their own private cooperative currency notes
correct_answer_text: They pool deposits from member farmers, use those deposits as collateral to obtain a large loan from a bank, and then lend to members for seeds, implements, and tube wells
explanation: Members pool deposits. With these deposits as collateral, the cooperative obtains a large loan from the bank. These funds are used to provide loans to members. Once these loans are repaid, another round of lending begins.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Beyond financial self-reliance, what crucial social transformation do Self-Help Groups (SHGs) facilitate for rural women?
option_a: Women are trained to serve in overseas foreign diplomatic corps
option_b: Regular meetings provide an empowering platform to discuss and act on social issues such as health, nutrition, hygiene, and domestic violence
option_c: Women are appointed as permanent judges of the high court
option_d: Women are exempted from domestic civil law jurisdictions
correct_answer_text: Regular meetings provide an empowering platform to discuss and act on social issues such as health, nutrition, hygiene, and domestic violence
explanation: SHGs are the building blocks of organisation of the rural poor. Not only does it help women become financially self-reliant, the regular meetings of the group provide a platform to discuss and act on a variety of social issues such as health, nutrition, domestic violence, etc.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Prem writes a cheque of ₹50,000 to Salim drawn on his State Bank of India account. When Salim deposits this cheque in his own Punjab National Bank account, what financial transaction occurs?
option_a: ₹50,000 is debited (transferred out) from Prem's SBI account and credited into Salim's PNB account through the interbank clearing system without any physical cash handling
option_b: Prem's house is automatically mortgaged to the Punjab National Bank
option_c: Salim must travel to Mumbai to collect gold coins from the Reserve Bank
option_d: The cheque is converted into a twenty-year government treasury bond
correct_answer_text: ₹50,000 is debited (transferred out) from Prem's SBI account and credited into Salim's PNB account through the interbank clearing system without any physical cash handling
explanation: A cheque allows direct book-entry transfer: money is transferred from one bank account to another bank account without any physical currency changing hands, making transactions safe and efficient.

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Cheap Credit as an Engine for National Development
question_text: Why is the availability of 'cheap and affordable formal credit' considered crucial for a country's economic development?
option_a: It eliminates the need for citizens to work or produce goods
option_b: It forces commercial banks to forgive all international foreign debts
option_c: It replaces all income taxes with private bank loans
option_d: It allows enterprises and small farmers to borrow, invest, establish new manufacturing units, expand output, and generate incomes without falling into debt traps
correct_answer_text: It allows enterprises and small farmers to borrow, invest, establish new manufacturing units, expand output, and generate incomes without falling into debt traps
explanation: Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development. High cost of borrowing means a large part of earnings is spent to repay the loan, leaving little for investment. Affordable credit promotes new businesses, agricultural investments, and employment.

subject: Social Science
question_text: To ensure equitable growth, what two vital credit policy reforms must the government and RBI pursue simultaneously?
option_a: Abolish all commercial banks and nationalize private gold jewellery
option_b: Force all rural farmers to borrow exclusively from private urban moneylenders
option_c: Expand overall formal lending in rural areas and ensure that formal credit is distributed more equally so that the poor can benefit from cheaper loans
option_d: Ban cooperative credit societies from operating in villages
correct_answer_text: Expand overall formal lending in rural areas and ensure that formal credit is distributed more equally so that the poor can benefit from cheaper loans
explanation: First, the formal sector must expand lending to replace moneylenders. Second, formal credit must be distributed equitably so that poor households, who currently get 85% of loans from expensive informal sources, receive affordable bank credit.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why are commercial banks willing to lend to Self-Help Groups even when the individual members possess no land or assets for collateral?
option_a: Because the entire group assumes collective responsibility for loan repayment, and any non-repayment by a member is followed up seriously by other members
option_b: Because the central government guarantees 100% reimbursement on any defaulted loan
option_c: Because SHG members are required to deposit foreign stocks as security
option_d: Because bank managers receive direct personal bonuses from SHG meetings
correct_answer_text: Because the entire group assumes collective responsibility for loan repayment, and any non-repayment by a member is followed up seriously by other members
explanation: The group is responsible for repayment. Any case of non-repayment of loan by any one member is followed up seriously by other members in the group. Because of this feature, banks are willing to lend to poor women organized in SHGs even without collateral.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Rama works as an agricultural labourer in Sonpur. During several months when there is no farm work, she borrows from her employer at 5% interest per month (60% annually). Unable to repay, she is forced to work for him at wages far below market rates. This scenario illustrates:
option_a: Formal banking credit facilitating upward economic mobility
option_b: Debt bondage and informal credit exploitation where the borrower is trapped in subservience due to unpayable compounded interest
option_c: A cooperative credit arrangement functioning under RBI guidelines
option_d: Corporate equity financing in rural agricultural markets
correct_answer_text: Debt bondage and informal credit exploitation where the borrower is trapped in subservience due to unpayable compounded interest
explanation: In NCERT’s Sonpur example, Rama borrows from her employer at 5% per month and repays by working for him. She often takes a fresh loan before the earlier one is repaid and remains dependent on the employer. The text describes exploitative dependence and labour-linked repayment; it does not calculate compound interest.
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 3, Section 3.3 (Case of Rama)

subject: Social Science
subtopic: Why RBI Mandates Priority Sector Lending
question_text: According to NCERT, why does the RBI supervise the lending activities of commercial banks?
option_a: To ensure that banks lend not only to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers
option_b: To guarantee that every borrower receives a loan regardless of repayment capacity
option_c: To prevent banks from accepting deposits from urban households
option_d: To set the same interest rate for every loan in India
correct_answer_text: To ensure that banks lend not only to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers
explanation: NCERT explains that the RBI monitors formal sources of loans and checks that banks lend not only to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers. Specific Priority Sector Lending categories and targets are set through RBI directions and may change over time; they are not the point being tested here.

subject: Social Science
question_text: Why do landless labourers and urban informal workers often fail to get loans from formal commercial banks even if they want them?
option_a: The law prohibits commercial banks from accepting currency notes from manual labourers
option_b: Formal bank branches are barred from serving Indian citizens
option_c: Bank computers cannot process loans less than ₹1 crore
option_d: They cannot produce formal salary slips, tax returns, land title records, or asset collateral demanded by bank documentation procedures
correct_answer_text: They cannot produce formal salary slips, tax returns, land title records, or asset collateral demanded by bank documentation procedures
explanation: Bank loans require proper documentation (proof of employment, salary slips, land title deeds) and collateral. Absence of collateral and documentation is one of the major reasons preventing the poor from getting bank loans.

subject: Social Science
question_text: How does a bank-to-bank digital payment such as UPI or NEFT relate to demand deposits?
option_a: They instruct the banking system to transfer funds from the payer’s bank account to the recipient’s bank account without using paper currency
option_b: They create new currency notes issued by private payment companies
option_c: They are unrelated to bank accounts and always settle through physical cash
option_d: They convert every bank deposit into a fixed deposit automatically
correct_answer_text: They instruct the banking system to transfer funds from the payer’s bank account to the recipient’s bank account without using paper currency
